To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the effects of prior detections on the estimation of detection probability, abundance, and occupancy can be large.

(a) the probability of detecting a species is affected by the number of detections that have occurred prior to the survey, (b) the probability of detection is affected by the species-specific detection history, and (c) these effects can be incorporated into the estimation process by using the detection history as a covariate in a generalized linear model.

(1) the probability of detecting the presence of an individual in a sample unit is not constant over space, time, or sample units; (2) detection probability can be affected by the presence of other individuals in the sample unit; and (3) the presence of other detected individuals in a sample unit affects estimates of detection probability, abundance, and occupancy.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the estimation of population parameters from data that are subject to imperfect detection, such as those collected in a line transect survey.
developing and applying statistical methods for estimating detection probability, abundance, and occupancy in the presence of heterogeneity and imperfect detection.

the development of methods and models that can be used to make inferences about the abundance of species, the detection probability of those species and the occupancy of those species, when the data are collected using multiple visits to the same sampling locations.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the detection probability of a species in a given survey area is the product of three components: 1) the probability of detecting a given individual of the species (detection probability of a single individual); 2) the probability of observing a given individual of a species (detection function of an individual); and 3) the probability of an individual belonging to the species (differential detection probability of a given individual).
there is no single best estimator for detection probability, abundance or occupancy.

, in a situation where a species is known to be present in a region, the use of a single detection probability model is sufficient to estimate detection probability and abundance, but the use of multiple models is required to estimate occupancy.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown that prior detections are a major source of bias in the estimation of abundance and occupancy and that this bias is likely to be present in a large number of studies.
we have shown that the use of prior detections in estimating detection probabilities, abundance and occupancy is a very useful approach that can be applied to a wide variety of data.
we can estimate occupancy and abundance from a single survey, but we need to be cautious about interpreting the results if there are prior detections.
The main takeaway from our work is that
prior detections can have a substantial effect on estimates of detection probability, abundance, and occupancy.
the prior probability of detection is a crucial parameter in occupancy models, and that the prior probability should be estimated from data.

the presence or absence of a species in an area may not be the best indicator of the true occupancy of that species, especially when there are many species present and detection probability varies among them.
